opts: Iatrogenic from a mismanaged third stage; neurogenic shock first, then haemorrhagic shock
Spontaneous inversion with haemorrhagic shock alone and no neurogenic component at all
Associated with placenta previa, producing septic shock with rigors and hypotension
Caused by uterine fibroids, with cardiogenic shock from acute left ventricular failure
exp: The commonest cause is mismanaged third stage; the initial neurogenic shock from stretching the pedicles is followed by haemorrhagic shock.

opts: Instrumental delivery, breech extraction, obstructed labour, tachysystole and high parity
Anaemia, gestational diabetes and an uncomplicated twin pregnancy
Placenta previa, placenta accreta spectrum and a previous caesarean scar
Chorioamnionitis, tocolytic therapy and a prolonged latent phase in labour
exp: Traumatic PPH follows tears and lacerations from operative delivery, malpresentation, obstructed or very fast labour and a large baby.

opts: OP: flat lower abdomen, limbs near the midline, heart in the flank — OA: convex abdomen with the limbs behind
OP: convex abdomen with the limbs behind — OA: flat lower abdomen, limbs near the midline, heart in the flank
OP: heart loudest in the midline — OA: heart in the flank with a flat lower abdomen below the umbilicus
OP: limbs in the flank with the heart in the midline — OA: bulging flanks with limbs felt on both sides
exp: In occipito-posterior the deflexed head leaves the lower abdomen flat, brings the limbs forwards and pushes the fetal heart out to the flank.

opts: The interlacing middle layer of myometrium, whose fibres compress the vessels as the uterus contracts
The round ligament, which anchors the uterus and kinks the ovarian vessels after delivery
The internal cervical os, which closes and compresses the cervical branch of the uterine artery
The decidua basalis, whose spiral arteries thrombose spontaneously after separation of the placenta
exp: The middle myometrial fibres act as living ligatures; when they fail to contract and retract, the sinuses bleed and atonic PPH follows.

opts: A chronic form of twin-to-twin transfusion through tiny anastomoses, with anaemia and polycythaemia but no fluid discordance
An acute severe form of twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome with sudden polyhydramnios in both sacs
A complication confined to dichorionic twins in which one placenta has a velamentous cord insertion
A complication of cord entanglement in monoamniotic twins that causes sudden death of both twins
exp: TAPS is chronic slow transfusion through anastomoses under 1 mm: the haemoglobin gap is large but the liquor volumes stay normal.

opts: Above 3.0 mm, or above the 95th percentile for the crown-rump length
Above 1.5 mm, or above the 50th percentile for the crown-rump length
Above 6.0 mm, or above the 99th percentile for the crown-rump length
Above 10.0 mm, or above the 99.9th percentile for the crown-rump length
exp: Nuchal translucency up to 3.0 mm (or below the 95th percentile for the CRL) is regarded as normal at 11 to 13+6 weeks.

opts: Low forceps: station +2 or more without reaching the perineum — outlet forceps: scalp visible at the introitus with the skull on the pelvic floor
Low forceps: at the level of the ischial spines — outlet forceps: station +1 with the head still above the pelvic floor
Low forceps: crowning with the head distending the perineum — outlet forceps: station +2 or lower inside the cavity
Low forceps: any station with the head not yet engaged — outlet forceps: the head still above the level of the ischial spines
exp: Low forceps are the commonest type and are applied at station +2 or more; outlet forceps are only used when the scalp is visible.

opts: Trisomy 16, which is always lethal in early embryogenesis
Trisomy 21, which is the commonest trisomy seen among liveborn infants
Trisomy 18, which is the commonest trisomy causing loss in the second trimester
Trisomy 13, which is the commonest trisomy associated with holoprosencephaly
exp: Trisomy 16 accounts for about a third of first-trimester losses and is incompatible with life; trisomy 21 is commonest at birth.

opts: More than 30 minutes after the delivery of the baby
More than 15 minutes after the delivery of the baby
More than 60 minutes after the delivery of the baby
More than 10 minutes after the delivery of the baby
exp: A third stage longer than 30 minutes is a prolonged third stage, and active intervention is considered once that time has passed.

opts: The first twin: a vertex first twin allows vaginal delivery whatever the second twin is doing
The second twin: any non-vertex second twin means both babies are delivered by caesarean section
The larger twin: whichever twin weighs more determines whether a caesarean is needed
The placental site: an anterior placenta makes a vaginal delivery of twins impossible
exp: The presentation of the first twin governs the plan; a breech or transverse second twin can often still be delivered vaginally by an expert.

opts: Wrapping the baby's lower body in a warm moist towel so the cord is not handled and vasospasm is avoided
Suprapubic pressure applied to the fetal head to keep it flexed during delivery of the after-coming head
Fundal pressure applied by an assistant to push the shoulders down through the pelvic brim
Rotating the fetal trunk through 180 degrees to bring the shoulders into the oblique diameter
exp: The Savage technique keeps the baby warm and prevents handling of the cord, since touching it provokes vasospasm and fetal distress.

opts: (Fundal height in cm minus n) times 155, where n is 12 above the spines and 11 below
(Fundal height in cm plus n) times 155, where n is 12 above the spines and 11 below
Fundal height in cm times 155, minus n, where n is 12 above the spines and 11 below
(Abdominal circumference in cm minus n) times 155, where n is 12 above the spines and 11 below
exp: Johnson's formula subtracts 12 when the head is above the ischial spines and 11 when it is engaged, and multiplies the result by 155.

opts: Commonest in monochorionic diamniotic twins, least common in monoamniotic, and not seen in dichorionic twins
Commonest in dichorionic twins with two separate placentas, and never seen in monochorionic twins
Commonest in monoamniotic twins because of cord entanglement, and never in monochorionic diamniotic twins
Equally common in every type, since transfusion depends on cord insertion rather than chorionicity
exp: Deep arteriovenous anastomoses in monochorionic diamniotic placentas drive TTTS; without shared circulation the syndrome cannot occur.

opts: The baby hangs by its own weight, then suprapubic pressure with the feet swung towards the mother's abdomen delivers the head
Two fingers are placed in the baby's mouth and traction is applied to the shoulders to flex the head
Piper's forceps are applied to the after-coming head while the body rests along the operator's arm
The baby's back is held upwards and the trunk is rotated to bring the head into the transverse diameter
exp: Burns-Marshall relies on controlled hanging with suprapubic pressure and swinging the body upwards to deliver the head by flexion.

q: Structures felt on vaginal examination — complete breech : frank breech : knee : footling.
opts: Complete: heel, anus and ischial tuberosities — frank: anus and tuberosities — knee: knees — footling: feet
Complete: feet only — frank: knees — knee: heel and anus — footling: anus and tuberosities
Complete: anus only — frank: feet — knee: heel — footling: knees
Complete: sacrum and anus — frank: feet — knee: anus — footling: knees
exp: The more the legs are extended, the less is felt: complete breech gives heel, anus and tuberosities, footling breech gives only the feet.

opts: Preterm labour, pre-eclampsia, postpartum haemorrhage, cord prolapse and malpresentation
Gestational diabetes alone, with no effect on the course of labour or delivery
Hyperemesis gravidarum alone, with no increase in risk later in the pregnancy
Iron deficiency anaemia alone, since only the maternal blood volume is affected
exp: Overdistension of the uterus and a large placental mass explain the whole spectrum of increased obstetric risk in twins.

opts: Sex, blood group, HLA type and physical phenotype, although the fingerprints remain different
Sex alone, since blood groups and HLA types are always different between monozygotic twins
Blood group alone, because sex and HLA types can differ even between monozygotic twins
Nothing at all, since monozygotic twins differ genetically as much as any two siblings
exp: Monozygotic twins share the whole genome, so sex, blood groups, HLA and phenotype match; fingerprints differ because they are formed by the environment.

opts: An aberrant artery-to-artery anastomosis through which the pump twin perfuses the acardiac twin in reverse
Deep arteriovenous anastomoses of the kind that produce classic twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome
Superficial venous anastomoses that allow a slow transfusion between the two circulations
Complete absence of any anastomosis, so each twin keeps an entirely separate circulation
exp: TRAP needs an artery-to-artery anastomosis: deoxygenated blood from the pump twin reaches the acardiac twin first and stunts its development.

opts: The lock closes easily and both blades lie equidistant from the sagittal suture along the occipito-mental diameter
The blades overlap slightly in the midline over the region of the anterior fontanelle
One blade lies over the face and the other over the occiput to grip the head firmly
The handles sit at 90 degrees to each other because the head is lying transversely
exp: Correct application means the lock closes without force, the blades sit symmetrically along the occipito-mental diameter and the sagittal suture is midway.

opts: Prolonged or precipitate labour, induction or augmentation, instrumental delivery and general anaesthesia
Epidural analgesia, delayed cord clamping and active management of the third stage
The left lateral position, ambulation during labour and continuous support from a companion
Oral fluids in labour, intermittent auscultation and delayed admission to the labour ward
exp: Intrapartum risk factors exhaust or damage the uterus and birth canal; the other options are neutral or protective measures.

opts: Second vertex: vaginal delivery — second breech: assisted breech — second transverse: internal podalic version in theatre
Every combination is delivered by caesarean section once the first twin has been born vaginally
Every combination can be delivered vaginally by an experienced operator without preparation
Caesarean section for a breech second twin only, since version is never attempted for a transverse lie
exp: When the first twin is vertex, a vertex or breech second twin can usually be delivered vaginally, and a transverse second twin by version and breech extraction.

opts: Deliver the first twin vaginally, then internal podalic version followed by breech extraction under anaesthesia in theatre
External cephalic version of the second twin, then an oxytocin infusion to deliver vaginally
Immediate caesarean section for the second twin as soon as the first twin has been born
Wait for spontaneous delivery of the second twin without any intervention for up to two hours
exp: Breech extraction is performed in theatre under anaesthesia, because all the manoeuvres are done by the operator with no maternal effort.

opts: Fetal biometry, liquor volume in each sac and Doppler for hydrops and abnormal waveforms
Cervical length alone, since transfusion does not affect growth or liquor volume
Placental grading alone, which predicts transfusion before any fetal change appears
Fetal sex determination alone, since chorionicity is already known from the first scan
exp: Surveillance looks for the consequences of unbalanced transfusion: growth discordance, liquor discordance, abnormal Doppler and hydrops.

opts: A previous preterm birth, a cervical length of 25 mm or less, and as an adjunct to cervical cerclage
Only in a twin pregnancy, whatever the cervical length or the obstetric history
Only after preterm prelabour rupture of membranes has already occurred
Only when there is vaginal bleeding from placenta previa in the third trimester
exp: Progesterone is given for a previous preterm birth, an incidental short cervix, or alongside cerclage in a classic history.

opts: A breach of the maternal-fetal interface lets fluid into the circulation, causing pulmonary vasospasm and then coagulopathy
A hypotonic uterus fails to compress the placental bed, causing haemorrhage, sepsis and renal failure
Placental abruption releases thromboplastin into the circulation, producing coagulopathy alone
Cord prolapse compresses the umbilical vessels, producing fetal hypoxia with no maternal effects
exp: Erratic contractions breach the interface and open venous sinuses; the fluid then causes pulmonary vasospasm, cardiac failure and consumptive coagulopathy.

opts: Weight loss of 5-6 kg at birth, then 2-3 kg from diuresis, with a very high cardiac output for 24-48 hours
Polyuria with a weight gain of 2 kg and hypokalaemia from rapid sodium retention
An immediate weight loss of 10 kg with a persistently low cardiac output for two days
Oliguria with hypernatraemia and a falling fibrinogen from postpartum coagulopathy
exp: Blood loss and diuresis account for early weight loss, and the cardiac output stays very high for one to two days, which matters in heart disease.
